title: When Anyone Can Build a Course, the Real Job Is Deciding Which Ones Shouldn't Exist
author: Hardman, Philippa
summary: AI has split the L&D role in two: production work (Data and Doing) now belongs to AI, while Deciding -- judging which interventions should exist and are pedagogically sound -- remains irreducibly human. The bottleneck in learning design has shifted from time to build to quality of judgment: a team can generate ten courses in an afternoon, but almost no one can look at a business problem and correctly determine that training is not the answer. Three things are required for genuine L&D professional judgment: deep learning expertise, specific business context, and human accountability for impact -- none of which AI can supply, because accountability requires a named person staking professional credibility on a decision. AI gets progressively better at procedural judgment but cannot inhabit professional judgment proper, defined as the willingness to be answerable for a decision. An experiment with a Fortune 500 client describes a four-agent workflow (Problem Framing, Behaviour Change Design, Quality, KPI Tracking) structured around human Deciding gates between every stage. The author ends with a practical exercise: map every task in a current project to Data, Doing, or Deciding, then decide what to delegate and what to protect.
points: * The L&D job has split: production (Data and Doing) belongs to AI; judgment about whether learning is the right intervention at all belongs to the human practitioner. * AI can produce plausible learning content; it cannot tell you which version will actually change behavior, because that requires expertise in cognitive load, retrieval, transfer, and motivation. * Professional judgment is structurally different from procedural judgment: it involves accountability, refusal, and stakes-bearing -- features that are definitionally unavailable to a model. * The smarter AI gets at procedural judgment, the more clearly the human-only zone clarifies itself: not the cognitive work, but the answerability. * Agents should gather, draft, and surface options, then stop; nothing moves forward until the human makes the judgment call at each Deciding gate.
quotes: The biggest AI risk that L&D faces isn't that it gets left behind: it's that we build more -- and flood the organisation with meh-quality content nobody needed in the first place.

Almost nobody can look at a business problem and decide that training isn't the answer here -- and be right. And almost nobody can stake their professional reputation on that refusal, year after year.
AI can recommend, but it cannot be accountable. Accountability is the structural reason professional judgement carries weight in organisations.

The question we've been asking for the last two years -- how do I get faster at building? -- was the wrong one. The real question is: can I look at fifteen AI-generated learning assets and decide which three are worth scaling?
